keyVerseText: And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse;
rootMeaning: The name Βοόζ (Boóz), of Hebrew origin בֹּעַז (Bôʻaz), conveys the idea of "fleetness" or strength. This root sense emphasizes vigor and stability, qualities that go beyond the mere English transliteration "Booz." The original Hebrew name also holds significance as both a personal name and a symbol, being the name of a prominent ancestor of David and a pillar in Solomon's temple, which suggests firmness and support.
usageInScripture: The word Βοόζ appears three times in the New Testament, consistently translated as "Booz," with one occurrence specifying "which was the son of Booz." This consistent usage highlights the name's role as a proper noun identifying a key Israelite figure. The limited but focused occurrences underscore its importance in genealogical contexts, particularly linking Old Testament heritage to New Testament lineage.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Βοόζ as more than a name but as one rooted in strength and reliability enriches our appreciation of God's providential plan through history. Boaz, as an ancestor of David and thus in the Messianic line, embodies God's faithfulness in preserving His covenant people. His role as a kinsman-redeemer reflects Christ's redemptive work, providing a foreshadowing of salvation. Recognizing the original meaning grounds believers in the reality that God's redemptive purposes are both powerful and steadfast.
keyVerseReflection: Matthew 1:5 states, "And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse." Here, the name Booz connects the genealogy of Jesus to faithful individuals whose lives demonstrate God's providence and grace. The presence of Boaz in this lineage highlights the continuity of God's redemptive plan from the Old Testament into the New, reminding us that Christ's coming fulfills promises rooted in the strength and faithfulness embodied by Boaz.
